blood pressure control is simple. It
helps your kidneys get rid of extra
sodium. And sodium holds on to water.
More sodium leads to more water in the
bloodstream, which leads to more
pressure inside your arteries. Think of
it like this. If your arteries are
garden hoses and you push more water
through them, pressure rises. Potassium
helps turn the faucet down. It tells
your kidneys, "Let go of some sodium."
When sodium leaves, water leaves with
it, and pressure drops. That's the main
way potassium lowers blood pressure, but
it does something else, too. Potassium
helps blood vessel walls relax slightly,
and that means the hose gets a little
wider. A wider hose leads to less
pressure. Now, here's the main problem
when it comes to potassium and blood
pressure. Most adults, especially those
over the age of 50, don't get enough
potassium in their diets alone. The
recommended amount for potassium for men
is around 3,400 mg and for women, it's
around 2,600 mg. Most people just don't
reach that. It's not because people

diets are extremely high in sodium and
low in whole foods. Good food sources of
potassium include avocados, spinach,
beans, lentils, yogurt, salmon, sweet
potatoes, and regular potatoes. Now,
let's talk about results. Studies show

a lot of sodium in their diet already. I

note about potassium and this is even

60. If you have chronic kidney disease,

medications like ACE inhibitors or ARBs,

if kidneys cannot clear potassium

a potentially fatal heart rhythm where
